title: Ancient Greece: From Hemlock to Bucephalus
description: A teacher's death, a grove of learning, a prince, and a horse afraid of its shadow—five steps into the tutors of conquerors.

questions.question: After Socrates drank hemlock in 399 BC, which student turned their conversations into the dialogues that still teach philosophy?
questions.explanation: Socrates wrote nothing down. Almost everything we "hear" him say is Plato ventriloquizing his teacher—and sometimes arguing with him.

questions.question: Plato founded a school in a sacred grove outside Athens named for the hero Akademos. What was the school called?
questions.explanation: Every "academy" since borrows the name. Aristotle's later school, the Lyceum, and Epicurus's Garden were the rivals.

questions.question: Which future philosopher studied at Plato's Academy for about twenty years—then spent a career disagreeing with him?
questions.explanation: He arrived around age 17 and stayed until Plato died in 347 BC. "Plato is dear to me," a later paraphrase goes, "but truth is dearer still."

questions.question: King Philip II of Macedon hired Aristotle to tutor which teenage prince?
questions.explanation: From about 343 BC, Aristotle taught the boy who would carry Greek culture from Egypt to the edge of India—and name cities after himself along the way.

questions.question: As a boy, Alexander tamed a horse no one else could ride by turning its head toward the sun—away from its own shadow. What was its name?
questions.explanation: He later named a city in modern Pakistan for the horse: Bucephala. When Bucephalus died, Alexander mourned him like a friend.

imageHint: Marble columns and the legacy of Athens

easterEgg.title: Afraid of its shadow
easterEgg.text: Plutarch says young Alexander noticed Bucephalus spooked at his own shadow, so he turned the horse's head toward the sun. He later named a city in modern Pakistan for the horse: Bucephala.
